title: Electrical Power Systems: From Generator to Socket
description: How electrical power is carried from a power station to a power point and kept in balance on the way, with Australia's National Electricity Market as the working example. You calculate power, power factor, three-phase loads and transformer losses, and judge how grids are held at 50 Hz, protected, and changed by solar and batteries.
audience: A curious adult or a student who has done simple DC circuits and the physics of induction. They know voltage, current, resistance and power, and that a transformer changes voltage by a turns ratio, but not what RMS, power factor or three-phase mean in practice, and not how a whole grid is run. The course explains protection and household safety so that learners understand it, and it never teaches electrical work, which the regulator's household pages leave to licensed electricians.
outcomes: You'll be able to read an AC supply: convert between peak and RMS values, read a period, a frequency and a phase angle, and check a voltage against Australia's 230 V tolerance.
You'll be able to find the real, reactive and apparent power of a load and size a power factor correction for a lagging load.
You'll be able to find the line and phase voltages, currents and power of a balanced three-phase load.
You'll be able to rate a transformer, find its efficiency from its losses, and estimate how line loss changes when the voltage changes.
You'll be able to relate poles, speed and frequency for generators and motors, and compute the slip of an induction motor.
You'll be able to predict how grid frequency moves when generation is lost, put the layers of frequency control in order, and read a NEM dispatch.
You'll be able to say what a fuse, a breaker, a relay, an earth connection and a safety switch each protect against, and when a householder should call a licensed electrician.
You'll be able to read a blackout timeline and separate the trigger, the weaknesses and the protection that acted.
You'll be able to judge what limits rooftop solar on a street, and match storage, curtailment, transmission and demand shifting to a variability problem.

modules.summary: What an AC value means, and how real, reactive and apparent power and power factor decide what a supply has to carry.

modules.title: Three-phase supply, transformers and transmission

lessons.title: Reading an AC supply
lessons.objective: Read the peak, RMS, period and frequency of an AC supply from a rating or a waveform, and say what a phase angle between voltage and current means for a load.

concepts.title: RMS value
concepts.summary: The effective value of an AC voltage or current is the DC value that produces the same heating, and for a sine wave it is 0.707 of the peak.

concepts.title: Period and frequency
concepts.summary: The period is the time of one cycle and the frequency is the number of cycles per second, so 50 Hz has a 20 ms period.

concepts.title: Phase difference
concepts.summary: Two waves of the same frequency can cross zero at different times, and the shift is measured in degrees of a 360 degree cycle.

misconceptions: 230 V means the voltage swings between plus and minus 230 V. It is an RMS value, so the peak of a sine wave of that size is about 325 V.
RMS is the average of the waveform. The average over a full cycle of a sine wave is zero; RMS is defined by heating effect, from squaring, averaging and taking the root.
A phase angle means the load is faulty or wasteful. It means the current peaks earlier or later than the voltage, which inductive and capacitive loads always cause.
sequence: Start from a heater on 230 V AC and on 230 V DC: they give the same heat, which is what the RMS value means.
Build RMS from the squaring, averaging and root steps on one cycle of a sine wave, then give the conversions: peak is 1.414 times RMS.
Show that supply voltages are quoted as RMS, and read Australia's nominal 230 V with its tolerance (plus 10 percent and minus 6 percent from 2000, plus or minus 10 percent from 2022).
Period and frequency: 50 Hz is 20 ms per cycle, so 5 ms is a quarter of a cycle.
Phase difference: lead and lag between two waves, in degrees, with 'in phase' as zero.
Set up the next lesson: an inductive load makes the current lag the voltage, and that shift decides how much of the current does useful work.
examples: Nominal 230 V RMS has a peak of 230 x 1.414 = 325 V.
A wave with a peak of 340 V has an RMS value of 340 x 0.707 = 240 V.
Tolerance from 230 V: plus 10 percent and minus 6 percent gives 216.2 V to 253.0 V; plus or minus 10 percent gives 207.0 V to 253.0 V.
At 50 Hz one cycle is 20 ms, so a current that crosses zero 5 ms after the voltage does lags by 5/20 x 360 = 90 degrees.

figures.shows: One cycle of a sine wave with the peak, RMS and peak-to-peak levels drawn as lines, in switchable views for a 230 V supply and a 12 V supply. The 340 V case is left to the questions.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the two supplies and the three labelled levels.

figures.shows: Two sine waves of the same frequency shifted by 0, 60 and 120 degrees, with the zero crossings marked and 'leads' and 'lags' labelled. The 90 degree case is left to the questions.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the three shifts.

questionPlan.sample: Mains in an Australian home is nominally 230 V RMS. What is the peak voltage of the sine wave, in volts?
An oscilloscope shows a sine wave with a peak of 340 V and a period of 20 ms. What is its RMS value, in volts?

Australia's nominal supply voltage is 230 V. The tolerance was plus 10 percent and minus 6 percent from 2000, and plus or minus 10 percent from 2022. A meter at the point of supply reads 212 V RMS. Which statement is right?
choices: Inside the 2022 range, outside the older range
Outside both ranges
Inside both ranges
Cannot be judged, because the meter might be showing peak
questionPlan.answer: Inside the 2022 range, outside the older range

distractors.option: Outside both ranges
distractors.mistake: Applying the old minus 6 percent limit (216.2 V) to the new standard, whose lower limit is 207 V.

distractors.option: Inside both ranges
distractors.mistake: Treating the old tolerance as symmetric.

distractors.option: Cannot be judged, because the meter might be showing peak
distractors.mistake: Doubting that mains voltages are quoted as RMS, which they are by convention.

questionPlan.sample: At 50 Hz, a load current crosses zero 5 ms after the voltage does. By how many degrees does the current lag?
A heater is rated for 230 V RMS. Why is RMS the value used for the rating, and not the average?
choices: It gives the heating that the same DC voltage would give
It is the value the voltage reaches most often
Over a full cycle the average of a sine wave is larger than the RMS value
It is the peak value divided by two
questionPlan.answer: It gives the heating that the same DC voltage would give

distractors.option: It is the value the voltage reaches most often
distractors.mistake: Reading RMS as a most-likely value.

distractors.option: Over a full cycle the average of a sine wave is larger than the RMS value
distractors.mistake: The full-cycle average is zero; the half-cycle average is 0.637 of peak, below the 0.707 RMS factor.

distractors.option: It is the peak value divided by two
distractors.mistake: Dividing by 2 and not by the square root of 2.

lessons.title: Real, reactive and apparent power
lessons.objective: Use the power triangle to find the real, reactive and apparent power of a load from its voltage, current and phase angle, and say which of the three a cable, transformer or generator has to be sized for.

concepts.title: Real power
concepts.summary: Real power P, in watts, is the average of voltage times current over a cycle and is the part that does work.

concepts.title: Reactive power
concepts.summary: Reactive power Q, in var, is energy that moves back and forth between the source and the magnetic or electric fields of the load, with no net transfer.

concepts.title: Apparent power
concepts.summary: Apparent power S, in volt-amperes, is RMS voltage times RMS current, and S squared equals P squared plus Q squared.

misconceptions: Apparent power is a loss. It is not dissipated; it measures the current the supply has to carry, which heats cables and transformers whether or not it does useful work.
Reactive power is used up like fuel. It is energy that goes out and comes back each cycle, so no net energy is consumed, yet the current that carries it still has to flow.
Real and reactive power add as plain numbers. They are at right angles on the power triangle, so S is the square root of P squared plus Q squared.
sequence: Multiply voltage by current at each instant for a resistive load, then for a load whose current lags by 90 degrees, and see the product go negative.
Average the product: that average is real power, and the swing above and below zero is reactive power.
Draw the power triangle with S as the hypotenuse, P along the base and Q upright, with P = S cos(phi) and Q = S sin(phi).
Work a case: 230 V, 10 A, current lagging so that the cosine of the angle is 0.8.
Why S matters: conductors, transformers and generators have to carry the whole current, so they are rated in kVA.
Read a rating plate or a supply transformer rating, and judge whether a stated load fits.
examples: A series circuit with R = 200 ohm, X = 50 ohm and a current of 2 A (the DOE handbook's case): P = 4 x 200 = 800 W, Q = 4 x 50 = 200 var, S = sqrt(800 squared + 200 squared) = 825 VA, power factor 0.97.
A factory draws 90 kW at a power factor of 0.70, so S = 90/0.70 = 129 kVA; a 100 kVA transformer cannot supply it.

figures.shows: Voltage, current and their product over one cycle, in views for a resistive load, a purely reactive load and a load lagging at an angle whose cosine is 0.8, with the area above the axis shaded one colour and the area below another.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the three loads and compare the shaded areas.

figures.shows: The power triangle with P, Q and S as arrows, drawn for two different angles.
figures.learnerAction: Switch the angle and watch S grow while P stays the same.

questionPlan.sample: A load draws 1.5 kVA of apparent power and 1.2 kW of real power. How much reactive power is that, in var?
A motor on 230 V draws 10 A, with the current lagging so that the cosine of the angle is 0.8. What real power does it take, in watts?
A workshop draws 90 kW at a power factor of 0.70 from a supply transformer rated 100 kVA. Can the transformer supply it?
choices: No, the load needs about 129 kVA
Yes, 90 kW is less than 100 kVA
Yes, because reactive power does not load a transformer
No, the load needs 90 kW plus 92 kvar, which is 182 kVA
questionPlan.answer: No, the load needs about 129 kVA

distractors.option: Yes, 90 kW is less than 100 kVA
distractors.mistake: Comparing watts with volt-amperes, which ignores the power factor.

distractors.option: Yes, because reactive power does not load a transformer
distractors.mistake: The current that carries reactive power still heats the windings.

distractors.option: No, the load needs 90 kW plus 92 kvar, which is 182 kVA
distractors.mistake: Adding P and Q as plain numbers instead of at right angles.

questionPlan.sample: A cable supplies a load whose rating plate shows 5 kW, 7 kVA. Which figure decides the current the cable must carry at 230 V?
choices: The 7 kVA
The 5 kW
Their average
Neither; current depends only on voltage
questionPlan.answer: The 7 kVA

distractors.option: The 5 kW
distractors.mistake: Using real power, which hides the extra current that carries reactive power.

distractors.option: Their average
distractors.mistake: Averaging two quantities that mean different things.

distractors.option: Neither; current depends only on voltage
distractors.mistake: Ignoring that current is set by the load at a given voltage.

lessons.title: Power factor and its correction
lessons.objective: Work out how a low power factor raises current and line loss, and choose and size a correction for a lagging load.

concepts.title: Power factor
concepts.summary: Power factor is real power divided by apparent power, the cosine of the phase angle, and is lagging for inductive loads such as motors.

concepts.title: Current and line loss
concepts.summary: For the same real power at the same voltage, current rises as 1 divided by the power factor and line loss as 1 divided by its square.

concepts.title: Power factor correction
concepts.summary: A capacitor supplies the reactive power an inductive load needs, close to the load, so that it does not have to flow from the generator.

misconceptions: A low power factor means the load uses less energy. The real power is the same; the load draws more current to deliver it.
The loss from a low power factor happens inside the load. It happens in the lines, transformers and generators that carry the extra current.
More capacitance always improves the power factor. Fixed capacitors supply reactive power whether or not the motors are running, so too much leaves a leading power factor and extra no-load loss.
Every low power factor is fixed with capacitors. Capacitors suit steady inductive loads; fast-changing loads and electronic loads with distorted current need other equipment.
sequence: 1 kW of real power needs 1 kVA at power factor 1 and 5 kVA at power factor 0.2.
From apparent power to current to loss: at power factor 0.7 the current is 1.4 times as large and the loss about twice.
Which loads have a low power factor: induction motors, transformers and fluorescent ballasts, against heaters and filament lamps.
Correction: a capacitor next to the motor supplies the reactive power, so the supply carries less.
Size a correction with the power triangle: find Q before and after, and subtract.
Choose among options: switched capacitor banks, a synchronous condenser, a static VAR compensator for fast-changing industrial loads, active correction inside electronic power supplies.
examples: 8 kW on 230 V: 34.8 A at power factor 1 and 43.5 A at power factor 0.8, which is 25 percent more.
A feeder at power factor 0.5 carries twice the current of one at 1.0 for the same real power, so its loss is 4 times as large.
100 kW at power factor 0.70 needs Q = 100 x tan(45.6 degrees) = 102 kvar; at 0.95 it needs 33 kvar; the capacitors must supply the difference, about 69 kvar.

figures.shows: Power triangle for a motor load, with a capacitor's reactive power drawn as an arrow in the opposite direction to the load's Q, in views for before correction, correct sizing and overcorrection, drawn for a different load from the one in the questions.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the three views and read the new apparent power.

figures.shows: Four loads (a steady bank of induction motors, a rapidly varying arc furnace, a computer power supply, a large spare motor) with their traits, left unlabelled for correction.
figures.learnerAction: None; the table is the material for the choice question.

questionPlan.sample: A load takes the same real power at power factor 0.8 as at 1.0, on the same voltage. By what percentage is its current higher at 0.8?
A feeder carries 100 kW. By what factor do its losses rise if the load's power factor falls from 1.0 to 0.5 at the same voltage?
A site draws 100 kW at a power factor of 0.70 lagging. How many kvar of capacitors bring it to 0.95, to the nearest kvar?
A factory's power factor is 0.70 lagging because dozens of induction motors run steadily all shift. Which correction fits?
choices: Capacitors connected near the motors
A bank of inductors in parallel
A thicker supply cable
Fewer, larger motors
questionPlan.answer: Capacitors connected near the motors

distractors.option: A bank of inductors in parallel
distractors.mistake: Inductors add to the lagging reactive power and make it worse.

distractors.option: A thicker supply cable
distractors.mistake: Treats the loss and not its cause; the reactive current still flows.

distractors.option: Fewer, larger motors
distractors.mistake: Lightly loaded large motors have a lower power factor, not a higher one.

lessons.title: Three-phase supply
lessons.objective: Find the line and phase voltages and currents of a balanced star or delta load, and the power it takes.

concepts.title: Three phases
concepts.summary: Three conductors carry the same frequency and voltage amplitude one third of a cycle (120 degrees) apart, so that their currents cancel in a balanced load.

concepts.title: Star and delta
concepts.summary: In a star connection the line voltage is the square root of three times the phase voltage; in a delta connection the line current is the square root of three times the phase current.

concepts.title: Three-phase power
concepts.summary: A balanced load takes P = root three x line voltage x line current x power factor, and the power is constant through the cycle.

misconceptions: A 230 V supply and a 400 V supply are two different supplies. They are the same three-phase supply, measured from one line to neutral and between two lines.
In a balanced load the neutral carries the sum of the three currents as a large current. The three currents cancel, so it carries almost none.
Three-phase simply triples the voltage. The line voltage is the square root of three, 1.73, times the phase voltage.
Line and phase quantities are the same in both connections. In star the voltages differ and the currents match; in delta the voltages match and the currents differ.
sequence: Draw three sine waves 120 degrees apart and show that at every instant they sum to zero.
Define line-to-neutral and line-to-line voltage, and the notation 230/400 V.
Show where the square root of three comes from on a phasor diagram.
Star and delta: which of voltage and current picks up the factor of 1.73.
Power of a balanced load, and why three-phase gives constant power and a rotating field for motors.
Why networks use it: the same power with 0.75 times the conductor, and why single-phase loads are spread across the three phases to keep the load balanced.
examples: From 230 V line-to-neutral, the line-to-line voltage is 230 x 1.732 = 398 V, written 230/400 V.
A balanced 15 kW motor at power factor 0.85 on 400 V takes 15000/(1.732 x 400 x 0.85) = 25.5 A per line.

Three 20 ohm resistors in delta on 400 V: each carries 20 A, each line carries 20 x 1.732 = 34.6 A, total power 3 x 400 x 20 = 24 kW; in star the same resistors on 400 V line voltage see 231 V and carry 11.5 A.

figures.shows: Three sine waves 120 degrees apart with their sum drawn as a flat line, and a phasor diagram with the line-to-line voltage as the difference of two phase voltages. Values for a 230 V supply are left off.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the waves, the phasors and an unbalanced case where one phase is loaded harder.
figures.placement: Opening and after the root-three argument.

figures.shows: A star and a delta load diagram with line and phase quantities labelled in symbols only.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between star and delta and read which quantity carries the factor.

questionPlan.sample: A three-phase supply measures 230 V from each line to neutral. What is the voltage between two lines, in volts?
A balanced three-phase motor takes 15 kW at power factor 0.85 from a 400 V supply. What is the current in each line, in amperes?
Three 20 ohm resistors are connected in delta across a 400 V three-phase supply. What current flows in each line?

distractors.mistake: Taking the line current equal to the phase current, which is true only in star.
Adding the three phase currents as plain numbers.
Using the star connection, where each resistor sees 231 V.

questionPlan.sample: Three identical heaters are connected one to each line and neutral of a four-wire supply. What current flows in the neutral?
choices: Almost none
The same as in one heater
Three times the current of one heater
The square root of three times the current of one heater
questionPlan.answer: Almost none

distractors.option: The same as in one heater
distractors.mistake: Ignoring that the three currents are 120 degrees apart and cancel.

distractors.option: Three times the current of one heater
distractors.mistake: Adding the currents as plain numbers.

distractors.option: The square root of three times the current of one heater
distractors.mistake: Applying the line-to-line factor where it does not belong.

lessons.title: Real transformers: ratings and losses
lessons.objective: Rate a transformer for a load, find its currents and efficiency from its losses, and say which losses change with load and which do not.

concepts.title: kVA rating
concepts.summary: A transformer is rated in kVA because voltage and current set its heating, whatever the power factor of the load.

concepts.title: Core and copper loss
concepts.summary: Core loss (hysteresis and eddy currents) is present whenever the transformer is energised; copper loss is I squared R in the windings and rises with the square of the load.

concepts.title: Efficiency
concepts.summary: Efficiency is output power over input power; distribution transformers typically reach 98 to 99 percent.

misconceptions: A transformer's losses grow in step with the load. Core loss is constant at every load and dominates at no load; only winding loss grows, and as the square of the current.
A transformer is rated in kW like a heater. It is rated in kVA, since the limit is current and voltage, not the useful power.
98 percent efficiency means losses do not matter. For a large unit the remaining 2 percent is a lot of heat, and a lightly loaded one is less efficient than a well loaded one.
A step-up transformer gives more power. An ideal one gives the same power at higher voltage and lower current; a real one gives slightly less.
sequence: Recall the ideal turns ratio from the physics course and say what an ideal transformer leaves out.
Two real losses: core loss from the alternating flux, copper loss from winding resistance.
Efficiency from output and losses, at full load and at light load.
Why the rating is in kVA, and how to find rated current for a single-phase and a three-phase unit.
Delta and wye connections of a three-phase transformer, and what they do to the line voltage.
Apply to a street: a lightly loaded pole transformer wastes most of its loss as core loss.
examples: A 500 kVA, 11 kV to 400 V three-phase transformer carries 500000/(1.732 x 400) = 722 A on the low-voltage side and 26.2 A on the high-voltage side.
At full load, 500 kVA at power factor 0.8 is 400 kW out; with 1.2 kW core loss and 6.0 kW copper loss the efficiency is 400/407.2 = 98.2 percent (invented figures).
At 10 percent load the copper loss falls to 6.0 x 0.01 = 0.06 kW, so efficiency is 40/41.26 = 96.9 percent; at half load it is 200/202.7 = 98.7 percent.

figures.shows: Core loss as a flat line and copper loss as a rising curve against fraction of full load for the invented 500 kVA transformer. No efficiency curve is drawn, so the efficiency questions are not answered by the figure.
figures.learnerAction: Read the two losses at chosen load fractions.

figures.shows: A delta-connected primary and a wye-connected secondary of a three-phase transformer, with line and phase voltages labelled in symbols.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between delta-delta, delta-wye and wye-wye.

questionPlan.sample: A 200 kVA three-phase transformer has a 400 V secondary. What is its rated line current, in amperes?
A transformer delivers 40 kW with a core loss of 1.2 kW and a copper loss of 0.06 kW at that load. What is its efficiency, in per cent?
A pole transformer rated 100 kVA serves four houses and rarely carries more than 10 kVA. Which loss accounts for most of its heat over a year?
choices: Core loss, which is present all the time
Copper loss, which grows with the load
Neither; it loses almost nothing at light load
Copper loss, because the current is small
questionPlan.answer: Core loss, which is present all the time

distractors.option: Copper loss, which grows with the load
distractors.mistake: Forgetting that copper loss follows the square of a small current.

distractors.option: Neither; it loses almost nothing at light load
distractors.mistake: Core loss does not depend on load.

distractors.option: Copper loss, because the current is small
distractors.mistake: Treating small current as large loss.

questionPlan.sample: A supplier rates a transformer 100 kVA. Why is it not rated in kW?
choices: Its limit is set by voltage and current, whatever the load's power factor
kW and kVA are the same unit
A transformer makes no real power
Heaters would otherwise be rated in kVA
questionPlan.answer: Its limit is set by voltage and current, whatever the load's power factor

distractors.option: kW and kVA are the same unit
distractors.mistake: Merging real and apparent power.

distractors.option: A transformer makes no real power
distractors.mistake: Confusing what it produces with what it limits.

distractors.option: Heaters would otherwise be rated in kVA
distractors.mistake: Not an engineering reason.

lessons.title: Why transmission uses high voltage
lessons.objective: Trace the path from a power station to a socket, say why each voltage step is there, and estimate how a change of line voltage changes the loss.

concepts.title: The voltage ladder
concepts.summary: Power is stepped up at the power station, carried on high-voltage lines, stepped down at substations to distribution voltage and again to 230/400 V for customers.

concepts.title: Loss against voltage
concepts.summary: For the same power and line, current falls as voltage rises and the resistive loss falls as the square of the current, so loss falls as 1 over the voltage squared.

concepts.title: Limits and HVDC
concepts.summary: Insulation, corona loss at very high voltage and reactive current on AC lines limit AC; HVDC wins on very long lines, submarine cables and links between grids that are not in step.

misconceptions: High voltage is used to push power harder. It is used to lower the current, which is what causes the loss.
Doubling the voltage halves the loss. Halving the current quarters it.
A thicker conductor is as good as a higher voltage. Loss falls only in proportion to the conductor's area, against the square for voltage.
All AC grids can simply be joined. Grids that are not in step need an HVDC link or a frequency converter, which is why Tasmania joins the mainland by Basslink.
sequence: Restate the physics course's result: the same power at ten times the voltage gives one tenth the current and one hundredth the loss.
Test it on real data: a 345 kV and a 765 kV line carrying 1000 MW over 160 km.
Why not go higher still: corona above about 2000 kV, insulation and equipment cost.
The ladder in the NEM: generation, long-distance lines (the pack gives 115 to 1,200 kV as the range), substations, 11 kV and 33 kV distribution as common in Australia, then 230/400 V.
Reactive current on long AC lines and HVDC: submarine cables, long lines and unsynchronised grids.
Trace a path and say what each box does.
examples: A line that loses 6 percent of its power at 66 kV loses 6 x (66/132) squared = 1.5 percent at 132 kV for the same power.
The pack's data: a 345 kV line over 160 km carrying 1000 MW loses 4.2 percent; the square law predicts 4.2 x (345/765) squared = 0.85 percent at 765 kV, inside the quoted 0.5 to 1.1 percent.
A 600 km undersea link between two grids that are not in step: HVDC.

figures.shows: A one-line diagram from a power station through a step-up transformer, a high-voltage line, a zone substation, a distribution feeder and a street transformer to a house switchboard, with voltage class labels.
figures.learnerAction: Select each stage to see its voltage class and what it does.
figures.placement: The reveal after the ordering question, which is asked first as a prediction; the diagram must not appear before it.

questionPlan.sample: A line loses 6% of the power it carries at 66 kV. For the same power over the same line at 132 kV, what percentage does it lose?
A source says a 345 kV line carrying 1000 MW over 160 km loses 4.2% of the power. Using the square law, what would a 765 kV line over the same distance lose, in per cent?
Two grids that are not in step with each other are to be joined by a 400 km undersea cable. Which choice fits?
choices: HVDC, which suits submarine cables and unsynchronised grids
AC at the highest available voltage
AC with a thicker conductor
Three-phase at a lower voltage
questionPlan.answer: HVDC, which suits submarine cables and unsynchronised grids

distractors.option: AC at the highest available voltage
distractors.mistake: Cable capacitance limits AC on long submarine runs.

distractors.option: AC with a thicker conductor
distractors.mistake: Loss falls only in proportion to conductor area, and the grids still would not be in step.

distractors.option: Three-phase at a lower voltage
distractors.mistake: Lower voltage raises the current and the loss.

questionPlan.sample: Put these stages of the path from a power station to a house in order, starting at the power station.
answer: Generator and step-up transformer at the power station
Zone substation stepping down to distribution voltage
Distribution feeder at 11 kV or 33 kV
Street transformer stepping down to 230/400 V

lessons.title: Speed, poles and frequency
lessons.objective: Relate the poles, speed and frequency of generators and motors, and use slip to tell an induction motor from a synchronous machine.

concepts.title: Synchronous speed
concepts.summary: A machine with P poles on a supply of frequency f has a rotating field that turns at N = 120 f / P revolutions per minute.

concepts.title: Synchronous machines
concepts.summary: A synchronous generator or motor locks into step with the field and turns at exactly synchronous speed; its field current sets voltage and reactive power, not frequency.

concepts.title: Slip
concepts.summary: An induction motor's rotor must turn slower than the field to have any current induced, and slip is the percentage difference.

misconceptions: A generator can turn at any speed and still make 50 Hz. Connected directly, its frequency is fixed by speed and poles.
An induction motor turns at synchronous speed. It cannot: with no relative motion there would be no induced current and no torque.
More poles means faster. More poles means slower for the same frequency.
Raising a grid-connected generator's field current raises the frequency. The grid fixes frequency; field current changes voltage and reactive power.
Motors are resistive loads. Their windings are inductive, which is why they have a lagging power factor.
sequence: Recall the coil in a field from the physics course and give one cycle per pair of poles passing a coil: N = 120 f / P.
Poles against speed at 50 Hz: 2, 4 and 6 poles.
Generators on a grid: same frequency, different speeds.
Field current: it controls the generator's voltage and reactive power, not the frequency.
Three-phase motor: the rotating field, slip, and a slip calculation.
Synchronous motor: locks in step, loses torque if overloaded, not self-starting; the link back to power factor.
examples: At 50 Hz a 2-pole machine runs at 3000 rpm and a 4-pole at 1500 rpm; a 6-pole at 1000 rpm.
A 4-pole 50 Hz induction motor running at 1440 rpm has slip (1500 - 1440)/1500 = 4 percent.
The handbook's 60 Hz case: a 2-pole motor at 3554 rpm has slip (3600 - 3554)/3600 = 1.3 percent.

figures.shows: A rotor with 2 and 4 poles, with the number of cycles per revolution counted on a waveform. The 6-pole case is left to the questions.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between 2 and 4 poles and count cycles per turn.

figures.shows: A rotating field and a rotor for an induction motor, with the rotor drawn lagging the field, and a speed ladder with the synchronous speed of a 4-pole motor marked and a rotor speed marked below it that is not the 1440 rpm used in the questions.
figures.learnerAction: Switch the load and watch the rotor fall further behind.

questionPlan.sample: A 6-pole machine is connected to a 50 Hz supply. What is its synchronous speed, in revolutions per minute?
A steam turbine drives a generator at 3000 rpm on a 50 Hz grid. How many poles does the generator have?
A 4-pole induction motor on a 50 Hz supply runs at 1440 rpm under load. What is its slip, in per cent?
The operator of a generator connected to a large grid raises its field current. What changes?
choices: Its voltage and reactive power output, while the frequency stays that of the grid
Its frequency rises
Its speed rises
Nothing; field current only matters to a stand-alone generator
questionPlan.answer: Its voltage and reactive power output, while the frequency stays that of the grid

distractors.option: Its frequency rises
distractors.mistake: Confusing excitation with the prime mover's torque; the grid holds the frequency.

distractors.option: Its speed rises
distractors.mistake: A synchronous machine on the grid turns at synchronous speed.

distractors.option: Nothing; field current only matters to a stand-alone generator
distractors.mistake: Central-station generators use field current to regulate reactive power.

questionPlan.sample: A motor turns at exactly its synchronous speed at every load and stops dead if it is overloaded. Which kind of motor is it?
choices: A synchronous motor
An induction motor
A motor with a very low slip
A motor whose slip is negative
questionPlan.answer: A synchronous motor

distractors.option: An induction motor
distractors.mistake: An induction motor always slips and slows gradually with load.

distractors.option: A motor with a very low slip
distractors.mistake: Low slip is still not synchronous speed.

distractors.option: A motor whose slip is negative
distractors.mistake: Mixing up motoring and generating.

lessons.title: Grid frequency and inertia
lessons.objective: Predict which way grid frequency moves when supply and demand differ, and explain how inertia sets how fast it moves.

concepts.title: Frequency as the balance signal
concepts.summary: In a synchronous grid every generator turns in step, so excess load slows them all and excess generation speeds them all, and the frequency shows the imbalance of the whole grid.

concepts.title: Inertia
concepts.summary: The spinning mass of synchronous generators supplies or absorbs the imbalance at once, which slows the first change in frequency and gives controls time to act.

concepts.title: Rate of change of frequency
concepts.summary: ROCOF, in hertz per second, is how fast frequency moves; it is larger when there is less inertia, for example when inverter-based generation replaces synchronous machines.

misconceptions: When demand exceeds supply the grid simply supplies more. The extra power first comes out of the generators' rotating energy, so they slow down.
Inertia stops frequency falling. It only slows the fall, so that governors and reserves have time to respond.
Frequency follows voltage. Frequency is set by speed, which is set by the balance of power.
The same loss is the same size of event on every grid. It is a larger share of a smaller grid, so it moves the frequency further.
Wind and solar make no difference to frequency. Inverter-connected generation has no rotating mass tied to the grid, so it adds no inertia unless it is built or controlled to imitate it.
sequence: A generator shaft: mechanical power in, electrical load out; excess load takes energy from the rotor and slows it.
In a synchronous grid every machine slows together, which is why frequency is a grid-wide signal.
Inertia as stored kinetic energy, and what happens in the first second after a trip.
Rate of change of frequency, and why high inverter-based generation means faster movement and more stress on protection.
Read a real event: Loy Yang A3 trips on 14 December 2017, frequency falls to 49.8 Hz in 20 seconds, and a battery responds.
Size matters: the same single failure is 6.4, 2.6 or 1.3 percent of average load in three US grids.
Ways to restore inertia: synchronous condensers, load that sheds, and batteries with inverters set to behave like a machine.
examples: Loy Yang A3 (560 MW) tripped at 1:58:59 am; by 1:59:19 the frequency had fallen to 49.8 Hz. If it started at 50.00 Hz, the average fall was 0.20/20 = 0.01 Hz per second.
Some grids require plants to tolerate a ROCOF of 1 to 4 Hz per second (as of 2017); the 20 second average above is a different, much gentler figure.
One failure can take 6.4 percent of average load in ERCOT, 2.6 percent in the Western Interconnection and 1.3 percent in the Eastern Interconnection.

figures.shows: A schematic (not to scale) of frequency against time after the same loss of generation on a high-inertia and a low-inertia grid, with a band around 50 Hz marked and the slower fall of the high-inertia grid labelled in words only.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the two grids.

figures.shows: The two data points of the 14 December 2017 event (the trip time and the 49.8 Hz reading 20 seconds later) on a time axis.
figures.learnerAction: Read the two points; the average rate is left to the question.

questionPlan.sample: A 600 MW generator trips and nothing else changes yet. What do the remaining generators' rotors do in the first seconds?
choices: Slow down, so the frequency falls
Speed up, so the frequency rises
Hold their speed, because the governors respond instantly
Stay at the same speed while voltage falls instead
questionPlan.answer: Slow down, so the frequency falls

distractors.option: Speed up, so the frequency rises
distractors.mistake: Reversing the sign of the imbalance; excess load slows the machines.

distractors.option: Hold their speed, because the governors respond instantly
distractors.mistake: Governors act after the rotors have already given up energy.

distractors.option: Stay at the same speed while voltage falls instead
distractors.mistake: Confusing frequency with voltage.

questionPlan.sample: Two grids of the same size lose the same 500 MW unit. Grid A has mostly synchronous generation; grid B has half the synchronous generation, replaced by inverter-based plant. What should you expect?
choices: Frequency falls faster in grid B
Frequency falls faster in grid A
Frequency falls at the same rate, since the imbalance is the same
Frequency does not fall in grid B because inverters respond faster
questionPlan.answer: Frequency falls faster in grid B

distractors.option: Frequency falls faster in grid A
distractors.mistake: Reversing the role of inertia.

distractors.option: Frequency falls at the same rate, since the imbalance is the same
distractors.mistake: Ignoring that inertia sets how fast the same imbalance moves the frequency.

distractors.option: Frequency does not fall in grid B because inverters respond faster
distractors.mistake: Fast response is not inertia and cannot act before the imbalance exists.

questionPlan.sample: A 560 MW unit trips at 1:58:59 am and the frequency has fallen to 49.8 Hz by 1:59:19 am. Suppose it started at 50.00 Hz. What was the average rate of fall, in hertz per second?
One failure removes 6.4% of average load in one grid and 1.3% in another. Other things equal, in which would you expect the frequency to move further?
choices: The grid where it is 6.4%
The grid where it is 1.3%
Neither; frequency depends only on the unit's size in megawatts
Both the same, since inertia scales with load
questionPlan.answer: The grid where it is 6.4%

distractors.option: The grid where it is 1.3%
distractors.mistake: Reading the bigger grid's larger absolute numbers as a bigger event.

distractors.option: Neither; frequency depends only on the unit's size in megawatts
distractors.mistake: The size relative to the whole grid is what matters.

distractors.option: Both the same, since inertia scales with load
distractors.mistake: The grids differ in inertia relative to the loss.

lessons.title: Frequency control and reserves
lessons.objective: Put the layers of frequency control in order of speed, match each disturbance to the layer that handles it, and say how the NEM dispatches generators and buys frequency services.

concepts.title: Layers of control
concepts.summary: Inertia acts at once, governor droop responds automatically, automatic generation control adjusts within several tens of seconds, reserves reach their promised output within about ten minutes, and replacement reserve takes 30 to 60 minutes.

concepts.title: Droop
concepts.summary: A governor with 4 percent droop changes output by 25 percent of its rating for each 1 percent change in speed, so generators share a frequency change in proportion to their size.

concepts.title: NEM dispatch and FCAS
concepts.summary: AEMO dispatches the cheapest offers every 5 minutes, sets the price at the highest offer needed, and buys regulation and contingency frequency control services to hold 49.85 to 50.15 Hz.

misconceptions: Reserve is spare plant sitting idle. Spinning reserve is headroom on units that are already running.
Every generator is paid its own offer price. All dispatched generators in a region receive the price set by the highest offer needed.
Frequency control is the same thing as energy dispatch. Dispatch is the five-minute plan; FCAS is a separate set of markets that holds frequency within seconds and minutes.
The same service handles slow drift and a large trip. Regulation FCAS handles small continuous variations and contingency FCAS handles large sudden changes.
sequence: The sequence after a large trip: inertia, droop response, automatic generation control, reserves, replacement.
Droop in numbers: 4 percent droop on a 3000 rpm turbine and what a 0.2 Hz fall asks of a 600 MW unit.
Reserves: spinning against non-spinning, the ten-minute rule, and why the reserve is at least the largest supplier.
The NEM: five-minute offers, cheapest first, price set by the highest offer needed.
FCAS: regulation against contingency, who may provide it, and the frequency performance payments from June 2025.
A battery as a grid service: the Hornsdale split between 10 minutes of grid services and 3 hours of trading.
examples: Droop: a frequency fall of 0.2 Hz on 50 Hz is 0.4 percent; at 4 percent droop that raises output by 0.4/4 = 10 percent of rating, so 60 MW from a 600 MW unit.
Merit order (invented offers): A 400 MW at $0, B 300 MW at $45, C 200 MW at $90, D 100 MW at $350. Demand of 850 MW takes A, B and 150 MW of C, so the price is $90 and B is paid $90 too.
Hornsdale phase one: 70 MW for 10 minutes (11.7 MWh) contracted to the government for grid services, and 30 MW for 3 hours (90 MWh) for trading.

figures.shows: A time axis from the instant of a trip to 60 minutes, with the five control layers drawn as bars from when each starts to act.
figures.learnerAction: None; it is the reveal after the ordering question, which is asked first as a prediction.

figures.shows: Four offers with quantity and price, and a demand line that can be moved between three values; the 850 MW case is left to the question.
figures.learnerAction: Move the demand line and see which offers are dispatched.

questionPlan.sample: A large generator trips. Put the responses in the order they act, fastest first.
answer: Rotor inertia of the synchronous generators

questionPlan.sample: A 600 MW turbine has a 4% droop setting. For every 1% change in speed its output changes by 25% of its rating. The grid frequency falls by 0.2 Hz from 50 Hz. By how many megawatts does the unit raise its output?
Offers for one 5-minute interval: A 400 MW at $0, B 300 MW at $45, C 200 MW at $90, D 100 MW at $350 per MWh. Demand is 850 MW. What price per MWh is set for the region?
Put each disturbance with the service that handles it.
Generator B offered at $45 per MWh and was dispatched in an interval whose regional price was $90. What does B receive for its energy?
choices: $90 per MWh
$45 per MWh
$67.50 per MWh, the average of the two
Nothing, because its offer was below the price
questionPlan.answer: $90 per MWh

distractors.option: $45 per MWh
distractors.mistake: Believing each generator is paid its own bid.

distractors.option: $67.50 per MWh, the average of the two
distractors.mistake: Inventing an averaging rule.

distractors.option: Nothing, because its offer was below the price
distractors.mistake: Reading a low offer as a rejected one.

lessons.title: Protecting against overcurrent
lessons.objective: For a described fault, say which device clears it (fuse, circuit breaker or relay with a breaker), which should operate first, and why a breaker has a short-circuit rating as well as a current rating.

concepts.title: Fault current
concepts.summary: A short circuit can draw many times the circuit's rated current, so the protection has to interrupt far more than the normal load.

concepts.title: Fuse, breaker and relay
concepts.summary: A fuse melts and is replaced, a breaker opens and can be reset, and a protective relay senses the fault and tells a breaker to open.

concepts.title: Coordination and zones
concepts.summary: Only the device closest to the fault should clear it, and protective zones overlap so that no fault falls between two of them.

misconceptions: A breaker's current rating tells you whether it is safe to use. Its interrupting capacity must also exceed the prospective short-circuit current at that point.
The device nearest the supply should always trip first. The one closest to the fault should clear it, so that the rest of the network stays on.
Fuses are obsolete. They clear faults very quickly, limit the energy let through, and need no mechanical maintenance, although a blown fuse must be replaced.
A fuse or breaker protects people from shock. They respond to large currents and do not see the small leak through a person.
sequence: Rated current against prospective fault current: typical domestic breakers interrupt 10 kA.
A fuse: a link that melts, fast, current-limiting, one shot, and what it cannot sense.
A breaker: detects by heat or magnetism, opens against an arc, resets, and carries an interrupting rating.
Relays and breakers on a large network: the relay senses, the breaker opens.
Protective zones around each element, with overlap.
Coordination: the branch device clears before the feeder device starts to act.
Read a case and choose the device.
examples: A domestic breaker rated to interrupt 10 kA on a circuit with a prospective fault current of 14 kA is under-rated for that point.
A fuse can clear a fault within a quarter cycle; a breaker takes about half to one cycle (at 50 Hz a cycle is 20 ms).
A fault in the overlap of two protective zones trips the breakers of both zones, a few more than strictly needed, which is accepted because a fault with no overlap could clear nothing.

figures.shows: A one-line diagram with a generator, a bus, a transformer and two feeders, each element with its protective zone drawn as a ring, overlapping at the breakers.
figures.learnerAction: Choose a fault location and see which breakers open.

questionPlan.sample: A breaker on a switchboard is rated to interrupt 6 kA. The prospective short-circuit current at that point is 14 kA. What is the problem?
choices: It may fail to interrupt the fault safely
None, because its current rating covers the load
It will open too slowly in an overload
None, because a fuse upstream always saves it
questionPlan.answer: It may fail to interrupt the fault safely

distractors.option: None, because its current rating covers the load
distractors.mistake: Confusing the load rating with the interrupting capacity.

distractors.option: It will open too slowly in an overload
distractors.mistake: Interrupting capacity is about faults, not overloads.

distractors.option: None, because a fuse upstream always saves it
distractors.mistake: Assuming protection upstream makes the rating irrelevant.

questionPlan.sample: A fault occurs in a branch circuit that is fed from a feeder, which is fed from the main supply. Each level has protection. Which should clear it, and why?
choices: The device closest to the fault, so the rest stays on
The main supply device, because it carries the most current
All three together, for safety
The feeder device, because it is in the middle
questionPlan.answer: The device closest to the fault, so the rest stays on

distractors.option: The main supply device, because it carries the most current
distractors.mistake: Choosing the biggest device, which would drop everyone.

distractors.option: All three together, for safety
distractors.mistake: Not understanding coordination.

distractors.option: The feeder device, because it is in the middle
distractors.mistake: No reason for a middle choice.

questionPlan.sample: A fault falls in the region where two protective zones overlap, and the breakers of both zones open. Why is the overlap accepted?
choices: Without it, a fault between zones would trigger no protection
It halves the clearing time
It lets the relays share one breaker
It is a design fault that is usually corrected
questionPlan.answer: Without it, a fault between zones would trigger no protection

distractors.option: It halves the clearing time
distractors.mistake: Overlap does not speed anything.

distractors.option: It lets the relays share one breaker
distractors.mistake: Not what overlap is for.

distractors.option: It is a design fault that is usually corrected
distractors.mistake: Overlap is deliberate.

questionPlan.sample: Put each description with the device it describes.

lessons.title: Earthing and safety switches
lessons.objective: For a described household fault, say which protection acts, what it does and does not protect against, and when the answer is to call a licensed electrician.

concepts.title: Automatic disconnection
concepts.summary: Exposed metal parts are connected to earth so that a fault to them becomes a current large enough for the breaker or fuse to clear.

concepts.title: Safety switch (RCD)
concepts.summary: A residual-current device compares the current out on the line with the current back on the neutral and opens when the difference, typically 30 mA, shows a leak to earth, within about 30 milliseconds.

concepts.title: What each device does
concepts.summary: Circuit breakers protect wiring from overload and short circuit, safety switches protect people from leakage shocks, and surge diverters protect equipment from voltage spikes; none replaces the others.

misconceptions: A circuit breaker protects you from electric shock. It responds to large currents; ESV states that circuit breakers do not act as safety switches for personal protection.
A safety switch makes every shock harmless. It does not see a shock between line and neutral, or an overload, and it only protects the circuit it is connected to.
If a safety switch does not trip when tested it is fine. A test that leaves the lights on means it may have failed and needs a licensed electrician.
Old wiring is safe once a safety switch is fitted. Degraded insulation and overloaded circuits start fires that a safety switch does not prevent.
The earth wire carries current in normal use. It exists to give a fault current a path so that protection operates.
sequence: A shock needs current through a person; a few tens of milliamperes is enough to be dangerous, which a 16 A breaker cannot notice.
The RCD: line current out, neutral current back, the difference is the leak.
Earthing: metal casing connected to earth so that a fault clears the breaker, and Australia's multiple earthed neutral system.
Limits of an RCD: it does not detect overload or a shock across line and neutral.
The three devices in an Australian switchboard: breaker, safety switch, surge diverter.
What householders and what licensed people do: what a failed test means, why old wiring needs inspection, and why only A grade electricians install wiring.
examples: Line current 8.000 A out and neutral current 7.940 A back is a 60 mA imbalance, above a 30 mA safety switch's threshold, so it opens.
A person touching line and neutral in a light fitting carries current through the load path, so the RCD need not see a leak.
ESV: fire brigades respond to more than 300 domestic electrical fires each year, many from degraded wiring.

figures.shows: A household circuit with line, neutral and earth conductors, a breaker, a safety switch drawn with its current-balance coil and an appliance, in switchable fault cases: leak through a person to earth, line-to-neutral short circuit, finger across line and neutral.
figures.learnerAction: Switch the fault and see which device sees it.

questionPlan.sample: Put each hazard with the device that is designed to deal with it.
A 30 mA safety switch is connected to a circuit. The line carries 8.000 A out and the neutral 7.940 A back. What happens?
choices: It opens, because 60 mA is leaking to somewhere other than the neutral
Nothing, because the currents are nearly equal
Nothing, because 8 A is below the circuit's rating
It opens only if the current exceeds the breaker rating
questionPlan.answer: It opens, because 60 mA is leaking to somewhere other than the neutral

distractors.option: Nothing, because the currents are nearly equal
distractors.mistake: The device responds to the small difference, not to the size of the current.

distractors.option: Nothing, because 8 A is below the circuit's rating
distractors.mistake: Treating it as an overload device.

distractors.option: It opens only if the current exceeds the breaker rating
distractors.mistake: Treating it as a breaker.

questionPlan.sample: A person touches the line and the neutral contacts of a light fitting at the same time, standing on a dry floor. Can you rely on the safety switch to open?
choices: No; the current goes through the person and the load, so it need not look like a leak
Yes; every shock is detected within 30 milliseconds
Yes; the safety switch measures the current in the person's body
No; safety switches only work on appliances with an earth pin
questionPlan.answer: No; the current goes through the person and the load, so it need not look like a leak

distractors.option: Yes; every shock is detected within 30 milliseconds
distractors.mistake: Believing a safety switch prevents all shocks.

distractors.option: Yes; the safety switch measures the current in the person's body
distractors.mistake: It measures only the difference between line and neutral.

distractors.option: No; safety switches only work on appliances with an earth pin
distractors.mistake: It works with any return path to earth.

questionPlan.sample: A householder presses the test button on a safety switch, and the lights on that circuit stay on. What does that show and what should happen next?
choices: The safety switch may have failed; a licensed electrician should investigate
It is working, because the test button does not cut power
Reset the main breaker and carry on
Open the switchboard and check the connections
questionPlan.answer: The safety switch may have failed; a licensed electrician should investigate

distractors.option: It is working, because the test button does not cut power
distractors.mistake: The test is meant to cut power to the circuit.

distractors.option: Reset the main breaker and carry on
distractors.mistake: Ignores the failed protection.

distractors.option: Open the switchboard and check the connections
distractors.mistake: Switchboard work belongs to a licensed electrician.

lessons.title: How a grid trips: South Australia, 2016
lessons.objective: Read a blackout timeline and separate the trigger, the weaknesses that let it spread and the protection that acted, then judge which statements about its cause the evidence supports.

concepts.title: Cascading failure
concepts.summary: A cascade is a chain in which each failure loads or disturbs the next, so that a local fault becomes a system event.

concepts.title: Trigger, weakness and response
concepts.summary: The trigger starts the event, weaknesses decide how far it spreads, and protection that operates correctly can still end in a blackout.

concepts.title: Restoring a grid
concepts.summary: A black start restarts generators with their own small sources, and restarting a state uses system restart services and the interconnectors.

misconceptions: A blackout has one cause. In 2016 the storm, the performance settings of wind farms, and the protection of the interconnector each played a part.
Protection that trips has failed. Here the automatic systems isolated plant to protect it, which is the system doing its job, and the blackout followed.
The upgrade work on the interconnector caused it. That was the first suspicion, but the work had been done earlier in the year.
A grid restarts by switching it back on. Power stations need their own power to start, which is why black start sources exist.
sequence: Set the scene: South Australia's grid, two interconnectors to Victoria, and a once-in-50-years storm.
The timeline in the 90 seconds before the blackout, from the first line trips to the interconnector shutdown.
The wind farm ride-through settings: nine ride-throughs in 120 seconds.
Classify each event as trigger, weakness or protective response.
Restoration: the Victorian interconnectors, system restart services, a circuit breaker that tripped on in-rush current, about 3 hours for Adelaide's suburbs.
What changed: the regulator's enforcement case in 2019, and in 2025 the AER reports AEMO's plans to reduce the number of synchronous generators required in South Australia from 2 to 1.
examples: Timeline items: 23 pylons damaged; a 66 kV line trips and resets; 47 seconds later a 275 kV line faults on two phases; a wind farm reduces output by 123 MW; the group of turbines that cannot ride through repeated faults drops out; the interconnector overloads and shuts down.
Result: about 850,000 customers lost supply, with suburbs back in about 3 hours and much of Adelaide by 10 pm.
Black start: Torrens Island could not restart itself and needed power from the Victorian interconnector.

figures.shows: The 28 September 2016 events on a time axis from the storm through the 90 seconds to the loss of the state, with restoration after.
figures.learnerAction: Select an event to see its type (the classification is left to the question).
figures.placement: After the ordering question, which is asked first from what the learner has read, and before the classification question.

questionPlan.sample: Put these events of 28 September 2016 in the order they happened.
answer: A violent storm damages 23 pylons and 275 kV lines fault
A wind farm reduces output by 123 MW and turbines that cannot ride through repeated faults drop out
The interconnector to Victoria overloads and shuts down
Almost the whole state loses supply
Restoration starts with power from the Victorian interconnectors

questionPlan.sample: Put each item in the right group for the 2016 event.
Which statement is best supported by the timeline and the reports?
choices: The storm began it, wind farm ride-through settings helped it spread, and protection then separated the state
Wind farms alone caused the blackout
The upgrade of the Heywood interconnector caused it
The protection should not have operated
questionPlan.answer: The storm began it, wind farm ride-through settings helped it spread, and protection then separated the state

distractors.option: Wind farms alone caused the blackout
distractors.mistake: Taking one contributing factor for the whole cause.

distractors.option: The upgrade of the Heywood interconnector caused it
distractors.mistake: The first suspicion; the interconnector had been upgraded earlier in the year.

distractors.option: The protection should not have operated
distractors.mistake: Treating protective action as the fault.

questionPlan.sample: After a total shutdown, why can a large power station not simply reconnect to the grid and restart?
choices: It needs its own power for pumps and fans, which a black start source provides
The grid refuses connections until frequency is exactly 50 Hz
Its generators cannot run without load
Regulations forbid it
questionPlan.answer: It needs its own power for pumps and fans, which a black start source provides

distractors.option: The grid refuses connections until frequency is exactly 50 Hz
distractors.mistake: Misdescribing synchronising.

distractors.option: Its generators cannot run without load
distractors.mistake: Not the issue here.

distractors.option: Regulations forbid it
distractors.mistake: Not a technical reason.

historyNotes: 28 September 2016: storm, about 3:50 p.m. loss of almost the whole state; about 850,000 customers affected (Wikipedia, citing AEMO's reports).

lessons.title: Inverters and rooftop solar
lessons.objective: Say what an inverter gives and does not give a grid, and judge what limits rooftop solar on a given street.

concepts.title: Grid-tie inverter
concepts.summary: A grid-tie inverter converts DC to AC matched to the grid's voltage, frequency and phase, and disconnects quickly if the grid goes down.

concepts.title: Two-way flow and voltage rise
concepts.summary: Rooftop solar makes distribution networks carry power in both directions, and midday export raises voltage along a feeder until inverters back off or trip.

concepts.title: Export limits
concepts.summary: Networks limit exports with a fixed static limit or a flexible limit that applies only when the local network needs it.

misconceptions: An inverter makes a house independent of the grid during a blackout. A grid-tie inverter disconnects when the grid goes down, so that it does not energise lines that people are repairing.
Solar adds inertia. A grid-following inverter has no rotating mass tied to the grid, and any inertial response has to be added by design.
The only limit on a street is the transformer. Voltage rise along the feeder and inverter behaviour also limit export.
Rooftop solar is sold through the market like a power station. It is not traded through the NEM, but it lowers the demand the market has to meet.
sequence: From DC panels to AC that matches the grid; why the inverter follows and does not lead.
No rotating mass: link back to inertia, and the battery with inverters set to behave like a machine.
The street: houses, a street transformer and a feeder, with midday export flowing the wrong way.
Three kinds of export curtailment: a static limit, voltage rise leading the inverter to trip, and a flexible limit.
The system view: midday demand has fallen in the NEM and evening peaks remain.
Safety and licensing: solar systems need servicing by a licensed A grade electrician.
examples: At December 2024 over 4 million Australian households had more than 22 GW of rooftop solar, 25 percent of capacity in the market.
A flexible export service lets customers export up to 10 kW for 95 percent of the year, against a static 5 kW, with limits only if grid stability is at risk.
Invented street: 30 homes each exporting 5 kW at midday put 150 kW into a 100 kVA street transformer, 1.5 times its rating at unity power factor.

figures.shows: A street with a transformer, a feeder and houses, with arrows for midday and evening flows and a voltage profile along the feeder, in views for no solar, solar on half the houses and solar on all.
figures.learnerAction: Switch the number of houses with solar and read the voltage at the far end.

questionPlan.sample: Which statement about a grid-tie solar inverter is right?
choices: It matches the grid's voltage, frequency and phase, and disconnects if the grid goes down
It supplies the grid with the same inertia as a steam turbine
It lets the house run normally during a grid blackout
It sets the grid frequency
questionPlan.answer: It matches the grid's voltage, frequency and phase, and disconnects if the grid goes down

distractors.option: It supplies the grid with the same inertia as a steam turbine
distractors.mistake: No rotating mass is tied to the grid.

distractors.option: It lets the house run normally during a grid blackout
distractors.mistake: Grid-tie inverters shut down when the grid is down.

distractors.option: It sets the grid frequency
distractors.mistake: It follows the frequency.

questionPlan.sample: Customers at the far end of a long feeder report that their solar inverters switch themselves down around midday, while customers near the transformer see no problem. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Voltage rise along the feeder from midday exports
The grid frequency is too high
The panels overheat at the end of the street
The transformer is too small for night loads
questionPlan.answer: Voltage rise along the feeder from midday exports

distractors.option: The grid frequency is too high
distractors.mistake: Frequency is common to everyone on the street.

distractors.option: The panels overheat at the end of the street
distractors.mistake: Location along the feeder would not matter.

distractors.option: The transformer is too small for night loads
distractors.mistake: The problem occurs at midday.

questionPlan.sample: 30 homes each export 5 kW at midday onto a street transformer rated 100 kVA, at unity power factor. What multiple of the transformer's rating is the reverse flow?

A network offers a static export limit of 5 kW, or a flexible limit of up to 10 kW for 95% of the year with limits only when grid stability is at risk. Which gives the customer more exported energy, and why?
choices: The flexible limit, because it only cuts exports when needed
The static limit, because it is guaranteed
They are equal, because both are capped
The static limit, because 5 kW is always available
questionPlan.answer: The flexible limit, because it only cuts exports when needed

distractors.option: The static limit, because it is guaranteed
distractors.mistake: The guarantee applies only up to 5 kW.

distractors.option: They are equal, because both are capped
distractors.mistake: The caps differ.

distractors.option: The static limit, because 5 kW is always available
distractors.mistake: Same mistake.

lessons.title: Storage, variability and curtailment
lessons.objective: Match a variability problem to storage, curtailment, a transmission upgrade or demand shifting, and tell power from energy when sizing a battery.

concepts.title: Power against energy
concepts.summary: A battery's power rating, in MW, is how fast it can deliver, and its energy rating, in MWh, is how long it can do so; the ratio is its duration.

concepts.title: What storage is for
concepts.summary: Batteries react within fractions of a second and suit frequency services and peak shaving, while pumped hydro is the largest form of grid storage and runs at an efficiency of 75 to 85 percent.

concepts.title: Curtailment
concepts.summary: Curtailment is an intentional cut in generation; it can be cheaper than building the lines or storage needed to use every megawatt-hour.

misconceptions: A bigger MW rating means more storage. MW is rate and MWh is amount; a 100 MW battery with 10 MWh runs out in six minutes.
Storage creates energy. Its efficiency is below 100 percent, so it returns less than it takes.
Curtailment is always a failure. It may be cheaper than the lines or storage needed to use all the output.
Solar only makes electricity cheaper. Midday prices are often negative and the evening peak remains, which is the duck curve.
sequence: Variability on all timescales: seconds to weeks; three routes to flexibility: storage, demand response, interconnection.
The duck curve and the Australian version: midday demand falling and negative prices.
Power and energy: Hornsdale at 150 MW and 194 MWh.
One battery with two jobs: 70 MW for 10 minutes of grid services and 30 MW for 3 hours of trading.
Pumped hydro: scale and efficiency, and the cost of building it.
Curtailment: causes, Australia's figure, and what reduced it elsewhere.
Choose a fix for each of four problems.
examples: Hornsdale: 150 MW and 194 MWh gives 194/150 = 1.3 hours at full power.
70 MW for 10 minutes is 70 x 10/60 = 11.7 MWh; 30 MW for 3 hours is 90 MWh.
In July 2025, 19,592 home batteries with a total nominal capacity of 356.6 MWh were installed: 356,600 kWh / 19,592 = 18.2 kWh each.

figures.shows: A net load curve (demand minus solar) with a deep midday belly and a steep evening neck, with a 1-hour and a 4-hour battery drawn as bands of power against time.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the two batteries and see which covers the evening ramp.

questionPlan.sample: A grid battery is rated 150 MW and 194 MWh. For how many hours can it deliver its full power, to one decimal place?
Part of a battery is contracted for grid services at 70 MW for 10 minutes. How much energy is that, in MWh?
In July 2025, 19,592 home batteries with a total nominal capacity of 356.6 MWh were installed in Australia. What is the average capacity per battery, in kWh?
A wind farm in a remote region is curtailed 12% of the time because its line to the city is full. Which change has the best evidence for cutting curtailment?
choices: A new transmission line
A battery at the city end
More turbines on the same line
A higher market price cap
questionPlan.answer: A new transmission line

distractors.option: A battery at the city end
distractors.mistake: The congestion is on the line before the city.

distractors.option: More turbines on the same line
distractors.mistake: Adds output to a full line.

distractors.option: A higher market price cap
distractors.mistake: Does not change the line's capacity.

questionPlan.sample: A planner says every megawatt-hour of curtailed solar is a failure that must be removed. What is the best reply?
choices: Sometimes using all the energy costs more than letting the surplus go
Curtailment is cheaper than storage in every case
Curtailment only happens because of faults
Curtailment is the same as load shedding
questionPlan.answer: Sometimes using all the energy costs more than letting the surplus go

distractors.option: Curtailment is cheaper than storage in every case
distractors.mistake: Overgeneralising.

distractors.option: Curtailment only happens because of faults
distractors.mistake: It is a routine tool.

distractors.option: Curtailment is the same as load shedding
distractors.mistake: Curtailment cuts generation; load shedding cuts demand.

courseCheck: A mixed check across the course: convert peak and RMS; find P, Q and S and the kVA a load needs; size a capacitor correction; line and phase quantities in a balanced three-phase load; transformer current and efficiency at light load; loss scaling with voltage and a choice between AC and HVDC; poles, speed and slip; the direction and speed of a frequency change from inertia; droop arithmetic and a merit-order price; which of fuse, breaker, relay, safety switch or surge diverter fits a hazard and what a failed safety switch test means; classify the events of a blackout; diagnose a street's solar limit; power against energy for a battery and the case for curtailment. Use at least two question kinds in each check, and set most questions on a case or a figure the lessons did not use.
platformNeeds: An AC waveform and power explorer: sliders for peak, frequency and phase angle, showing voltage, current and their product over a cycle and the power triangle. Fallback: the svg_figure views planned in lessons 1 to 3, with three or four fixed cases each.
A one-line diagram explorer where the learner picks a fault location and sees which zones and breakers act (lessons 10 and 12). Fallback: an svg_figure with three fixed fault cases.
A merit-order stack with a movable demand line (lesson 9). Fallback: a table of offers with three demand values.

A feeder voltage-profile figure with houses that can be switched to solar (lesson 13). Fallback: an svg_figure with three cases. A real one would need a source for voltage rise along a feeder, which the pack does not give.
A frequency-after-a-trip schematic with an inertia setting (lesson 8). The pack has no swing equation, so only a qualitative drawing is supported.
unverified: The pack has no swing equation or inertia-constant formula, so lesson 8 is qualitative apart from reading an event; do not add a ROCOF formula from memory.

The pack does not state that Australian three-phase supply is 400 V line to line; it gives 230 V nominal for Australia and 230/400 V as the pattern for 230 V countries. Lesson 4 infers the 400 V figure from the square root of three.

The pack gives no table of NEM transmission voltages. South Australian examples name 275 kV (Heywood) and 150 kV (Murraylink) and a 66 kV line; Australian distribution at 11 kV and 33 kV is from one Wikipedia sentence.

The 2016 blackout is Wikipedia's summary of AEMO's reports and the AER's later case. AEMO's own reports are not in the pack (aemo.com.au refused automated access). Cause is shown as several contributing factors, as the page shows it.
AEMO's naming of raise and lower contingency services is not explained in the pack, so lesson 9 uses only 'regulation' and 'contingency'.

Why midday export raises voltage along a feeder is not explained in the pack; the AER footnote only names 'voltage rise'. The mechanism (current through feeder resistance) is the course's own reasoning from lesson 6.

Anti-islanding rules for Australian inverters are not in the pack; the statement that grid-tie inverters disconnect when the grid goes down is general, and the pack's one regulatory mention is the US National Electrical Code.
The pack gives two test intervals for safety switches (every three months and every year) on ESV pages, and two RCD trip times (25 to 40 ms and 0.03 s). Questions should not depend on either.

Invented numbers, all marked as such in the plan: the 500 kVA transformer losses, the merit-order offers, the 30-home street with a 100 kVA transformer, the 100 kW power factor case, and the 90 kW factory.
The DOE handbooks date from 1992 and have scrambled equations; their prose and worked numbers are used. Their 98.2 percent transformer efficiency rounds from 98.1.
